title: The Person in Front of You Is Extraordinary
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer reports on trying her own '35 Questions for a Better Life Together' with six other people in Ojai, beginning with the question of what each wanted to be at five years old. She describes two hours of phone-free listening in which even long-time friends became more dimensional to her. From there she argues that when we forget how extraordinary the person in front of us is, we reduce people to categories such as employee, voter, client or problem to be solved. Systems built around categories produce one-dimensional responses, and every policy and organizational decision eventually lands in a human life. She suggests the five-year-old question is useful because it points to what someone cared about before conditioning arrived. The piece closes with three reflection questions and the claim that seeing begins again one person at a time.
points: A simple, structured evening of questions and attention made familiar people newly dimensional, showing how little it takes to see someone fully.
Categories like employee or demographic are useful but become harmful when systems are built around them instead of the person.
Every policy, funding priority and inherited rule is eventually experienced by a human being with a story.
The five-year-old question invites people to recover what delighted them before the world offered opinions about what was realistic.
quotes: For two hours on an ordinary Monday night, people relaxed and truly listened to one another.
What happens when we forget how extraordinary the person in front of us actually is?
These categories are useful. Sometimes they are necessary. But they are never the whole person.
When we see people one-dimensionally, it should not surprise us that we create one-dimensional responses.
Every system we create eventually lands in a human life. Every policy. Every organizational decision.
Because human flourishing cannot begin with an abstraction. It begins with seeing people fully enough to remember that no single circumstance tells us who they are.
And no system designed for human beings can truly serve them if it forgets their humanity along the way.
